paras: The mock hanging of Ned at Sherman, Wyoming, took place on 3 May 1882, when Sherman men hoisted a Black chore boy called Ned by a rope over a cigar theft. After a barn burned, pursuers caught him again; the Cheyenne Daily Leader reported a second use of the rope, which a Sherman resident denied.
Ned worked at Mr. Pillman's Summit and Sherman house; the Leader said four boxes of cigars were stolen from a saloon keeper, a Sherman letter five boxes and a suit of clothes.

According to the Leader, his captors strung him up 'for a moment or two' to frighten him, then told him to leave. The letter claimed Ned put the rope on himself, that it ran over a telegraph pole with about ten men on his end and six on the other, and that he was freed after promising to show where the goods were.

Later a barn on the edge of Sherman, which the letter said belonged to the hotel, burned with a valuable horse inside, and Ned was suspected of setting it. The Leader said men on a hand car found him in sheds toward Cheyenne and went through 'the formalities of a lynching', leaving him 'half choked'. The letter said he was found four miles east of Sherman and was 'well treated and no hanging as stated'.
Ned was turned over to the authorities, and Justice Roberts committed him to jail in default of $500 bond to the October term of court. No report of a trial was found.

The only coverage found ran in the Cheyenne Daily Leader, under the headline 'Twice in a Night'. Its first report presented the hoisting as fright followed by 'sage advice', called him "nigger" Ned, and did not criticize the men. Two days later it printed A. L. Sutherland's correction, which called the night 'our racket at Sherman' and stressed Ned's thefts.
The accounts differ over the stolen goods, who put the rope on Ned, where he was caught, and whether a second hanging occurred. Both versions come from the Sherman side; none is from Ned.

reader.title: Mock hanging of Ned at Sherman, Wyoming
bases: A group of Sherman men put a rope on Ned's neck and hoisted him to force admissions about a theft, and a pursuing party went through 'the formalities of a lynching' after a barn fire, but he was not killed and was turned over to the authorities [A1, A2].

Ned was hoisted by a rope and, by one account, half choked by men acting without legal authority over accusations of theft and arson, but both accounts say he survived and was handed to the authorities [A1, A2].

Both reports, in the same Cheyenne paper, agree on the theft accusation, the rope over his neck, the barn fire and his return to Sherman, but the Sherman letter denies that any hanging took place at the second capture [A1, A2].

accounts.label: Leader reporter
accounts.gist: Ned was strung up for a moment to frighten him after stolen cigars were found on him, then told to leave; after the barn fire a hand-car party found him in sheds toward Cheyenne, went through 'the formalities of a lynching', half choked him without getting a confession, and handed him to the authorities.

accounts.label: Sherman resident's letter
accounts.gist: Ned put the rope on his own neck, was hoisted over a telegraph pole until he promised to show where the goods were, burned the hotel barn after being released, and was found four miles east of Sherman, 'well treated' with 'no hanging'; he admitted hiding cigars near the barn and was committed to jail.

framing.detail: The Leader's first report, headlined 'Twice in a Night' with the subhead 'The Number of Times Nigel Ned was Strung up', described the hangings as fright and 'sage advice' and assumed Ned's guilt for arson, without condemning the men.
The Sherman letter, headlined 'True Inwardness of the Thing', called the night 'our racket at Sherman', said Ned had been 'in the habit of stealing', and denied any hanging at the second capture.

quotes: The party who caught the negro, in order to frighten him thoroughly, put a rope around his neck and strung him up for a moment or two.
A rope was procured and the formalities of a lynching gone through with it, but although half choked the negro refused to confess that he had set the barn on fire.
